paper_a.title: Hahn-Banach Theorem: a proof of the equivalence between the analytic and geometric versions

paper_b.title: Another proof of the analytic Hahn-Banach Theorem

metadata.description: Both papers concern the classical Hahn-Banach theorem and the relation between its analytic and geometric (separation) forms. Paper A proves the analytic↔geometric equivalence and, as its main contribution, derives the geometric version from the analytic one via a Minkowski-functional construction. Paper B provides 'another proof' of the analytic Hahn-Banach (in the complex case) by going in the opposite direction: it derives the analytic version from the geometric separation theorem through an auxiliary convex-functional lemma and a complex-linear decomposition. The shared sub-task — proving the analytic version from the geometric one — is realised by two genuinely different proofs (Paper A: PP421.3 via $A=\{x:p(y-x)<1\}$; Paper B: PP423.2 via $H,G\subset L\times\mathbb R$ in product space and Lemma LP423.2), making this a clean alternative-proof pair.

matches.explanation: Both define the standard semi-norm: a non-negative subadditive and absolutely homogeneous functional on a vector space. The two statements are textually different but mathematically identical; Paper A flags it as external/standard while Paper B re-states it as a paper definition, but the object is the same.

Paper A explicitly defines a hyperplane as a codimension-one subspace; Paper B uses hyperplanes throughout (in $L\times\mathbb R$) but never extracts an explicit definition node. The concept is implicit on the B side, so no L1 counterpart exists.

The Minkowski-functional definition is central to Paper A's main proof PP421.4 (geometric → analytic). Paper B never uses Minkowski functionals; instead it invokes Lemma LP423.2 (real Hahn-Banach via a convex functional). No B counterpart.

Paper A's inductive ordered family $({A},\preceq)$ is bookkeeping for the Zorn-based proof of analytic HB (PP421.1, which is cited rather than original). Paper B does not run a Zorn argument explicitly — it derives analytic HB from the cited geometric HB — so this auxiliary order has no B analogue.

Paper A's family $B$ of subspaces avoiding $A$ supports the Zorn-based proof of the geometric HB (PP421.2). Paper B treats geometric HB only as a cited result (TP423.1) and never instantiates this poset.

The cone $B=\bigcup_{\alpha>0}\alpha A$ is a paper-original construction inside Paper A's main proof PP421.4 (analytic → geometric via Minkowski functional). Paper B uses a completely different reduction (auxiliary convex functional, separation in $L\times\mathbb R$) so no analogous cone construction exists.

The balanced 0-neighborhood $D=(B-x)\cap(x-B)$ is part of Paper A's symmetrization step inside PP421.4. Paper B has no analogous construction — its 0-neighborhood base $\{V_n=U_n\cap(-U_n)\}$ in PSP423.5 plays a different role (defining a TVS topology to make $\varphi$ continuous), not symmetrizing a cone for a Minkowski functional.

All three nodes are the analytic Hahn-Banach extension theorem — dominate-by-seminorm, extend a linear functional from a subspace to the whole space. Paper A states the real case (TP421.1, marked external/classical). Paper B states a 'cited' form TP423.2 (over a general scalar field $\Phi$, also external) and proves the complex case TP423.3 as its main result. TP423.3 is an exact match in content; TP423.2 is the same theorem cited verbatim from Schaeffer.

Both are the geometric (separation) Hahn-Banach theorem: a linear subspace/manifold disjoint from an open convex set extends to a hyperplane disjoint from that set. Paper A's TP421.2 omits 'closed' on the hyperplane while Paper B's TP423.1 (citing Schaeffer) requires closedness, but the underlying classical statement is the same. Both are tagged external; the match is informational and does not by itself determine the relation type.

Paper A's headline theorem — 'analytic and geometric HB are equivalent in real TVS' — is its paper-original main result. Paper B does not state any equivalence theorem; it only proves one direction (geometric → analytic) and frames it as an alternative proof of the analytic version. Hence no L1 counterpart on the B side.

Zorn's Lemma is cited in Paper A (used in PP421.1 and PP421.2 for the classical Zorn-based proofs). Paper B does not invoke Zorn in any of its extracted nodes — it relies on the cited geometric HB instead. (External↔external trivial match suppressed per origin-aware filtering.)

'Minkowski functional is a continuous seminorm' is a standard external lemma used by Paper A inside PP421.4. Paper B never appeals to Minkowski-functional continuity; the analogous role on the B side is played by Lemma LP423.1 (convex functional continuity ⇔ upper semi-continuity), which is a different statement.

Paper B introduces 'convex functional' as a basic definition because its Lemma LP423.2 generalises the seminorm hypothesis to a positively homogeneous convex functional. Paper A only ever works with seminorms (DP421.1) and the absolute-value bound $|f|\leq p$, so it never needs this more general convex-functional notion.
Proof of LP423.1 (continuity ⇔ upper semi-continuity for convex functionals on a real TVS). This auxiliary continuity argument is paper-original to B and has no analogue in Paper A's proof pipeline.

Paper B's auxiliary lemma — a convex functional on a real TVS is continuous iff upper semi-continuous — is a paper-original technical tool used to make $\varphi$ continuous before applying geometric HB in PP423.2. Paper A has no analogous lemma; its proof path needs only the standard Minkowski-functional continuity (LP421.2).

Paper B's 'real Hahn-Banach extension via a convex functional' is a paper-original real-case lemma: it generalizes the seminorm hypothesis to a positively homogeneous convex functional and is the engine that drives PP423.3 via complex decomposition. Paper A has no convex-functional generalization — it works with seminorms throughout.
Structural propositions about $M=G+\bigcup_{\alpha>0}\alpha A$ are internal to Paper A's Zorn-based proof of geometric HB (PP421.2). No analogue in Paper B.
'$G$ is a hyperplane iff $E=G\cup M\cup(-M)$' is internal to Paper A's geometric-HB proof (PP421.2). Paper B has no analogous characterization.

This is the heart of the AP relationship. Paper A's PP421.3 derives the analytic HB from the geometric HB by separating the open convex set $A=\{x:p(y-x)<1\}$ from $\mathrm{Ker}(f)$ in $E$, recovering $g$ from the resulting hyperplane. Paper B accomplishes the same task but along a fundamentally different route: PP423.2 first proves a real-case extension via a convex functional by separating $H=\{(x,t):g(x)-t=1\}$ from $G=\{(x,t):\varphi(x)-t<1\}$ in the product space $L\times\mathbb{R}$ (the classical Bohnenblust-Sobczyk-style epigraph trick), then PP423.3 lifts to the complex case by the standard $g(x)=g_0(x)-ig_0(ix)$ decomposition. Same destination (analytic HB from geometric HB), genuinely different proofs — the canonical 'alternative proof' situation.

Composite L2-vs-L2 entry attached to the parent match (PP421.4 on A vs PP423.2+PP423.3 on B is not the right pairing here since PP421.4 goes the other way; this composite pairs Paper A's PP421.4 step DAG against Paper B's full main step DAG only as a structural cross-reference). Both proofs share recognisable phases — build a 0-neighbourhood (PSP421.2 vs PSP423.5–6), check continuity/seminorm properties (PSP421.3 vs PSP423.7), set up the linear functional on a privileged subspace (PSP421.4 vs PSP423.8), invoke the partner Hahn-Banach version (PSP421.6 vs PSP423.9), and conclude (PSP421.7–8 vs PSP423.10–12); Paper B further adds the complex decomposition (PSP423.13–16). The mappings are coarse and the granularities differ, hence low confidence; emitted as a single composite per the v2 L2 rule.
Paper A's classical Zorn-based proof of analytic HB. Paper B does not reproduce a Zorn-based proof; its analytic HB comes from the cited geometric HB via LP423.2 + complex decomposition.
Paper A's Zorn-based proof of the geometric HB. Paper B uses geometric HB only as a cited tool, so there is no corresponding proof on the B side.

Paper A's main contribution — deriving geometric HB from analytic HB via the Minkowski-functional construction (cone $B$, balanced $D$, seminorm $p$, functional $f$ on $S\oplus\langle x\rangle$, extension $g$, hyperplane $\mathrm{Ker}(g)$). Paper B never proves geometric → from analytic; it goes the opposite way. So this paper-original proof has no B analogue and is the strongest evidence that the two papers complement each other rather than compete.
Auxiliary remark inside Paper A's proof; remarks are excluded from compactness rules but listed here for completeness. (Per v2 spec, remark 'none' entries can be omitted; left in for transparency.)
Equivalence $|g|\leq p\Leftrightarrow A\cap\mathrm{Ker}(g)=\emptyset$ is a remark internal to Paper A's main proof and has no Paper B counterpart.
